title: Cranberry Sauce

drivers.name: Price increase (5.6%)
drivers.evidence: No lift observed in prior weeks with same price ($2.85); sales dropped to 4 in 2026-04-13 after price increase; historical promotions at lower discounts showed no sustained lift; noise-adjusted promotion effect is x1.0; price increase likely reduces demand.

adjustment.analysis: The baseline median is 8.3. The target week has no event, but a 5.6% price increase to $2.85. Past data shows no promotion in this week, but a 30% off promotion in 2026-02-23 drove sales to x1.48 vs baseline. However, the noise-adjusted estimate for all past promotions is x1.0, indicating no lasting uplift. The week after that promotion saw x0.68, but noise-adjusted x1.0. Price increases in prior weeks (2026-03-30, 2026-04-06, 2026-04-13) saw no lift, and sales dropped to 4. The classical model suggests no effect, which aligns with weak historical signals. A price increase likely suppresses demand. Given the evidence, the median is adjusted down slightly, with uncertainty in the spread.

  shelf price: 2.85 (+5.6% vs regular price 2.70)

STATISTICAL BASELINE (exponential smoothing of recent sales; it ignores events, promotions and prices):
  median 8.3 | 5%-95%: 0.0 - 18.5 | 10%-90%: 0.9 - 17.0

In the evidence below, 'vs baseline' = actual units / what this same baseline predicted for that week.
It is the multiplier that would have been right, so it maps directly onto median_multiplier.
This product's ordinary weeks already swing about +/-76% around the baseline, so a past effect smaller than that, seen only a few times, is mostly noise. The
'noise-adjusted estimate' is the effect shrunk toward x1.0 for that noise and the number of sightings.
